How to prepare for next year?

First off, good on you for thinking about next year in April! The biggest issue with people gardening or farming sustainably is they want immediate results.

Keep in mind that if you want to establish a new garden bed where there is grass or poor soil you will need to do some digging or tilling. Once your bed is nice and fertile, that's when digging becomes more damaging. If you want to pick a spot and mix in some horse poo. That's a great idea! I also highly recommend lasagna gardening aka sheet mulching. This is best done in the fall when leaves and straw are abundant and free (if you don't mind being the weird guy stealing leaves, I don't).

For your current garden, let your plants get nice and tall then mulch the fuck out of the ground in-between with something herbaceous like leaves or straw. This helps retain water, balance soil temps, and breaks down into humus.

Finally if you eschew my last few tips, cover crops. Find a seed for the season and just plant some cover crops, then mix them into the soil before they go to seed.

Basically, just add a fuck load of organic matter.

I'm not sure if daikon is a cover crop but I do know that for living mulch cover crops red clover, alfalfa, hairy vetch, or cow peas are excellent choices. Really you can't go wrong picking most anything in the legume family. There are some that work that aren't legumes though like: Barley, buckwheat, oats, rye, and winter wheat.

My guide is for the rocky mountains but it says for alfalfa you can sow in spring and turn under that fall or following spring, Barley, buckwheat, and oats you can sow in spring as well then turn under in the fall (with exception to oats with you turn in the spring). Rye and winter wheat you can sow in the fall and turn in the spring.

Alfalfa helps nitrogen levels, barley and rye add organic matter, buckwheat mellow your soil to make it easier to work with, and the oats and winter wheat help improve soil aggregation.

(This is all information from "Guide to Rocky Mountain Vegetable Gardening" by Robert Gough & Cheryl Moore-Gough, pg 103)

You are not wrong. One could not till it dig at all and still loosen soil, but it will take a long long time. Tilling and digging is good for getting things started. A nice established and fertile bed should not be tilled casually though.

One way to get rid of grass and weeds without killing the soil is to double dig. There is also a "stale bedding" method which is recommended after double digging to ensure the destruction of grass, weeds and grubs that eat roots plus it helps introduce oxygen into the soil. However it at the very least requires hand tilling (if you have a small bed) every couple weeks until fall.

Also I can't speak for the effectiveness of horse manure, however my reading all points toward the use sheep and goat manure or aged/composed chicken manure (so that there are lower nitrogen levels). Although as long as it comes from an herbivore I'm sure you're fine.
